implementation_notes: The standard library gives no page cache, so the structure is assembled: an unordered_map keyed by method + target + the header axes you vary on, a std::shared_mutex (C++17) so hits take only a shared lock while a miss re-renders under an exclusive one, and an entry holding the finished bytes, an ETag and a steady_clock expiry. Store the key as std::string, never as a string_view into a request buffer - those buffers are reused and dangling views are the standard trap - and keep bodies in std::shared_ptr<const std::string> or copy them out under the lock, because unordered_map rehash and erase invalidate references another thread may be writing. Most C++ HTTP services do not cache in-process at all: a Beast/Asio or framework handler emits Cache-Control/ETag and nginx or Varnish (both C) holds the shared cache, which keeps the header semantics in one place.
pitfalls: Rendering while holding the exclusive lock serialises the whole cache and turns it into the bottleneck it was meant to remove; render outside the lock and insert afterwards.

unordered_map invalidates iterators and references on rehash: move-assigning a body out of a node while another thread inserts can free the buffer mid-write - hold shared_ptr bodies and copy under the lock.
std::shared_mutex is neither recursive nor free on every platform; never lock it from the render path, and do not assume shared locking beats a plain std::mutex on a short critical section.
Keys and bodies grow with query strings: without an entry cap and expiry the table is a memory leak with a traffic-shaped trigger.
